2. US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)/ University of Hawai`i
Hawaiian Islands Fiber Link (HIFL) Project – Kaua`i Cable Landing Site at Nukoli`i
Beach Park and Kaua`i Community College
TMK: (4) 3-7-003:007 (por.); (4) 3-7-003-017 (por.); (4) 3-7-003:999 (Kūhiō Highway
ROW); and (4) 3-4-007:003 (por.)
Ms. Valenciano provided background on the project and the Section 106 process. She
explained that Section 106 is a federal regulatory review triggered using federal
funds, federal lands, or federal involvement, often in partnership with private
entities. The process allows State holders, Native Hawaiian Organizations, and other
consulting parties to comment on proposed projects, particularly regarding potential
impacts to historic properties and cultural resources. The purpose of the process is

to invite input from parties who may have knowledge of or concerns about impacts
to historic properties. She noted that the Commission is reviewing back-to-back
Section 106 projects. The current project under consideration is the Hawai`i Islands
Fiber Link project, involving the University of Hawai`i and the U.S., Army Corps of
Engineers. The proposed undertaking includes the construction, operation, and
maintenance of an interisland cable. She described the project components, which
include the offshore cable placed on the seafloor, onshore components, and cables
that connect along the highway to the landing sites. The primary landing locations
are at Kaua`i Community College and an area near Nukoli`i Beach. As part of project
preparation and due diligence, the applicant conducted an archaeological literature
review to identify previous studies in the project area. That review identified several
historic properties and sites associated with various features, including bridges and
plantation-era resources. These findings are documented in the agency’s letter and
accompanying report. Based on the results of the literature review, the agency
determined that additional information is needed and proposed conducting an
archaeological inventory survey to better assess the presence of historic properties
and to more clearly determine potential project impacts. The department
recommended that the Commission provide any comments, concerns, or knowledge
of historic properties in the project area at this time, as the Section 106 consultation
is ongoing and the project is moving forward.
Vice Chair Summers asked a question regarding the two telecommunications
projects, noting that they appear similar. She requested clarification on how the
projects differ, including whether they are commercial in nature, whether they
involve different companies, and why two separate cables are being proposed or
installed.
Ms. Valenciano responded that the question may be best directed to both project

consultants. She stated that, at a basic level, the projects are intended to support
internet infrastructure. She noted that she was not certain why there are two
separate projects and explained that it appears coincidental that two Section 106
projects with similar scopes are being reviewed at the same time.
Vice Chair Summers followed by stating that the issue may also be a question for the
County. She asked whether the projects involve different companies installing
infrastructure to provide internet service, and if so, whether the County has
considered combining the projects. She expressed concern about approving two
separate cable routes and landing sites that appear to follow similar paths, including
along the highway, and questioned why the infrastructure is not being consolidated.
She asked whether there are specific reasons preventing the projects from being
combined.
Ms. Valenciano responded that she did not have a definitive answer to the question.
She noted that in traditional telecommunications projects there is typically a process
that encourages co-location of facilities but stated that this project involves a
different type of communications infrastructure. She explained that she is not
familiar with the specific process or requirements that apply in this case.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked whether the contract location would interfere with
any existing ocean traffic.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa noted that many of the questions could be directed at the
consultant, who has more detailed information, and asked whether Ms. Valenciano
could clarify anything from the department’s perspective at this point.

With no one in the public to testify on this item, the Commission heard from Mara
Mulrooney, a principal and senior archaeologist with Pacific Legacy.
Ms. Mulrooney stated that his firm is a subconsultant on the project, which is a
partnership between the University of Hawaii and Ocean Networks. She noted that
the primary partners were unable to attend, said she would do her best to answer
technical questions, and offered to relay any questions to the broader project team.
Commissioner Remoaldo reiterated her earlier question, asking whether the
punchout location at 78 feet interferes with any existing ocean traffic.
Ms. Mulrooney responded that the project team does not anticipate any impact on
ocean traffic. She referenced the plan and profile views showing the proposed
landing near Nukoli`i Beach, noting that the punchout location is well offshore and
below the surface, crossing the shoreline at approximately 52 feet deep, with the
beach manhole located about 300 feet inland. She explained that the project design,
which uses horizontal directional drilling at set back mauka of the shoreline facilities,
was developed to minimize impacts to the sensitive shoreline area and to protect the
cable from potential damage by surface traffic.
Vice Chair Summers asked for clarification, confirming whether the cable would be
laid on the surface of the ocean floor and then, at a point offshore, descend to about
50 feet in depth, travel underground to the onshore site, and then come up on land.
Ms. Mulrooney confirmed that the cable will be surface laid on the ocean floor by a
ship and then transition to horizontal directional drilling to a beach manhole located
about 300 feet inland. She referred to the project profile diagram showing this
configuration and noted that the cable is approximately the size of a highlighter. She

added that the next step will be an archaeological inventory survey, including
subsurface testing at the beach manhole location, to ensure the project does not
impact archaeological, historical, or cultural resources.
Vice Chair Summers asked whether the cable connects to a junction box beneath a
manhole and then continues underground from that point.
Ms. Mulrooney confirmed that from the beach manhole the cable will continue in
underground conduit along Kaua`i Beach Road and Kaua`i Beach Drive, then connect
to existing overhead infrastructure along Kūhiō Highway to KCC, where the cable
landing station will be located within an existing campus building and tied into the
grid. She explained that the Hawaiian Islands Fiber Link project is a third-party,
“middle mile” infrastructure project not affiliated with a specific utility, intended to
provide connectivity to six Hawaiian Islands and access for all private providers. She
noted the aging condition of the state’s three existing cables, past their useful life,
and emphasized the urgency of these projects given the islands’ reliance on internet
connectivity.
Vice Chair Summers asked whether the three existing cables, once they are out of
service, remain in place or are removed.
Ms. Mulrooney responded that the three existing cables remain in place even after
they are out of service.
Vice Chair Summers asked whether there has been any discussion about placing the
infrastructure underground instead of using overhead delivery for this project.
Ms. Mulrooney stated that, while not an expert on overhead versus underground

delivery, the University of Hawai`i and Ocean Networks team designed the project to
limit ground disturbance. She noted that installing underground conduit would be
more costly and could potentially impact subsurface historic properties. Therefore,
the decision was made to use existing overhead infrastructure rather than placing
the cable underground all the way to the University of Hawaii.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked whether a monitor will be present on-site during any
construction or project work.
Ms. Mulrooney confirmed that both an archaeological monitor and a cultural monitor
are recommended to be on-site during construction for this project.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked for clarification, questioning whether the presence
of the monitors is only recommended or if it will be required.
Ms. Mulrooney explained that the requirement for monitors is determined by the
State Historic Preservation Division, not the consultants. She noted that having both
an archaeological and a cultural monitor on-site has been and will continue to be
their recommendation.
Vice Chair Summers asked for clarification, confirming that monitoring would occur
at the beach manhole but not along the horizontal directional drilling section from
the ocean floor to the manhole.
Ms. Mulrooney confirmed that a monitor will not be present during the horizontal
directional drilling from the ocean floor to the manhole. She explained that the
drilling process moves material upward, and archaeological concerns are primarily
within the first meter below the surface. To address this, subsurface testing will be

conducted as part of the archaeological inventory survey within that footprint, since
cultural resources are unlikely to be present at greater depths.
Chair Larson stated that this is a Section 106 consultation and asked whether the
group has any early-stage comments or recommendations regarding the treatment
of historical resources that should be sent to the applicants.
Commissioner emphasized the importance of monitoring at this location, noting that
during the original Nukoli`i development there was significant controversy regarding
burials, indicating that the area is known to have sensitive grounds.
Chair Larson summarized that the Commission appears to agree that the historical
and cultural monitoring is appropriate. She then called for a motion.

Vice Chair Summers moved to
recommend historical and cultural
monitoring throughout the project.
Commissioner Quinsaat seconded the
motion. Motion carried 8:0.

With no one in the public to testify on this item, the Commission heard from Bobby
Uyehara with Hawaiian Telecom and the Program Manager, as well as Brian Takeda,
consultant with R.M. Towill.

Mr. Takeda stated that the discussion would focus on the first phase of the project,
which involves geotechnical soil sampling.
Commissioner Remoaldo noted that while the bore holes are described as four inches
in diameter with a ground disturbance of 0.1 square feet, the project materials do
not specify the depth of the proposed boring.
Mr. Takeda explained that the project involves a total of three bore holes with bore
#1 reaching approximately 10 feet in depth, bore #2 approximately 20 feet, and bore
#3 approximately 50 feet. Each bore is expected to take no more than two to eight
hours to complete, and the work will be conducted sequentially over a period not
expected to exceed one to three days.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked how the locations of the proposed bore holes were
determined.
Mr. Takeda explained that the bore hole locations were identified based on the
proposed alignment of a horizontal directional drilling route extending from the
beach manhole toward deep ocean waters. He noted that the geotechnical bore
locations would not necessarily be on the exact alignment of the future directional
drilling bore but were selected to evaluate the underlying soil conditions along the
anticipated route.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked that since the final project alignment may differ from
the locations of the current bore holes, what would occur if findings were discovered
during the boring activities.

Mr. Takeda stated that various discoveries could occur during the boring activities,
and that an archaeologist would be present during the initial boring to monitor site
preparation and excavation. He noted that the archaeologist would observe and
examine the area as equipment is set up and work begins, though the exact depth
and procedures would be determined through further coordination with the State
Historic Preservation Division (SHPD). He added that these details would be outlined
in an archaeological monitoring plan to be reviewed by SHPD.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked whether the area shown on the handouts is within
the existing camping area or located elsewhere in the park, noting that the camping
area occupies one portion of the park while the remainder is used for picnicking.
Mr. Takeda responded that the area in question likely corresponds to the second
exhibit, which is depicted as a polygon with a small tip near the shoreline. He
explained that the polygon was intended to illustrate the area of potential effect of
the project.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked for clarification on whether the identified area falls
within the camping area or the picnicking area of the park.
Mr. Takeda stated that it is likely that a portion of the camping area may be affected
by the proposed work.
Vice Chair Summers noted that, according to page 4, one of the boring locations is in
the parking area, while another is under a tree in an area commonly used for
camping.

Commissioner Remoaldo asked how long it would take to complete the boring
activities and restore the area of potential effect afterward.
Mr. Takeda explained that most of the work would occur on bare ground with
minimal vegetation, and after boring, the removed material would be backfilled and
any excess disposed of at an approved County facility. He estimated that restoration
would likely take a few days to a week. For areas such as parking lot, where paved
surfaces might be affected, additional preparations would be required to restore the
pavement.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked for clarification on the expected appearance after the
work is completed, specifically how large the footprint would be for any equipment
or activities on the land portion.
Mr. Takeda stated that, practically, the boring work would leave little to no evidence
of activity once completed, aside from restoration efforts. He noted that there may
be small patches of new pavement, bare ground, or areas where grass or other
plantings need to be replaced, but over time these areas should return to their
existing condition.
Commissioner Remoaldo asked how large the land-based connection area would be
once the project is fully completed.
Mr. Takeda explained that once the project is fully completed and the equipment is
removed, the only visible evidence on the land portion

before the Commission is a zoning permit to construct a new exterior ATM, along
with related exterior and interior modifications to an existing bank building. She
noted that the Commission may recommend approval as proposed, approval with
conditions, denial, or deferral of the permit. She stated that the department
brought the item forward primarily due to the installation of a new exterior ATM on
the front of the building along Rice Street. While an exterior door and interior work
are also proposed, the department does not believe those elements affect the
historic character of the building. The department’s review focused on whether the
exterior ATM would result in an adverse effect on potential historic property and
whether mitigation measures were necessary. She noted that the building is not
listed on the State Historic Register but may be eligible under Criteria C.
Determining eligibility is complicated due to extensive renovations over time and
uncertainty regarding how much of the original structure remains. The building was
constructed in 1912 as one of the island’s first reinforced concrete buildings,
originally featuring single-story columns on the front and eastern sides. Major
renovations occurred in 1938, including a change to a double-pitched steep roof,
and again in the 1960s with significant interior and exterior alterations, including
façade changes, lava rock elements, and a drive-through teller window on the
eastern side. Ms. Valenciano added that zoning permit records show additional
exterior modifications over time, including conversion of the drive-through teller to
an ATM on the eastern side. While recent permits do not indicate major changes to
the front façade, historic photographs show that the front has been altered over
multiple remodels, aside from the concrete columns. Based on available research,
the department believes that the historic integrity of the building, except possibly
for the roof and front columns, has been lost or diminished. She further noted that
the department asked the applicant to consider placing the ATM on the eastern
side where one previously existed, but the applicant preferred the front location for
better weather protection. She concluded that the proposed work would not

adversely affect the historic property, as the building has undergone numerous past
renovations and the project is consistent with previous improvements.
With no one in the public to testify on this item, the Commission heard from
Thomas Knapp with Palms Hawaii Architecture.
Mr. Knapp noted that the agenda packet includes comparisons of floor plans and
exterior elevations over time, prepared by Ms. Valenciano, to illustrate the
building’s changes. He explained that this project is part of the Bank of Hawai’i’s
broader “Bank of Tomorrow” modernization program, aimed at updating branches
to align with current banking processes and anticipated market demand.
Chair Larson stated that the most significant change appears to be the installation
of an ATM kiosk at the front of the building.
Mr. Knapp clarified that the ATM will not be a kiosk but will be flush with the wall.
Chair Larson confirmed that this is the most significant change, and Mr. Knapp
added that this allows customers to access the ATM without entering the building.
Chair Larson referenced the earlier suggestion to place the ATM on the side of the
building to make it less intrusive and asked for clarification on how placing it on the
front provides better protection from the weather.
Mr. Knapp explained that during the 1963 remodel, a drive-up teller window was
added on the side facing the post office, which was later converted to a drive-thru
ATM. He noted that the branch does not intend to have a drive-thru, and placing a
walk-up ATM on that side would expose users to inclement weather, which is why
the front location was preferred.

Chair Larson asked if that side has an overhang.
Mr. Knapp replied that there is no significant overhang on that side, so users would
get wet. The proposed front location is within the colonnade on Rice Street,
providing protection.
Ms. Valenciano noted that Exhibit A in the Director’s Report includes photos of the
eastern side and front of the building. She explained that the eastern side currently
has a clean wall with no drive-thru teller or ATM. Historically, there were concrete
columns, but expansions created a solid wall with no overhang. In contrast, the
proposed front location will provide automatic protection from weather elements.
Chair Larson asked what currently exists in the area designated for the ATM and
whether that wall is original from 1912.
Mr. Knapp responded that the wall along the back of the colonnade has been
modified multiple times with glazing, windows, and infill walls, and that the specific
wall for the ATM was likely installed during the 1963 remodel.
Chair Larson noted that the 1963 remodel is already 60 years old. Mr. Knapp added
that the most recent interior remodel is 22 years old and somewhat dated.
Vice Chair Summers asked about the construction behind the proposed ATM
location, and Mr. Knapp replied that it is a metal stud and cement plaster wall.
Vice Chair Summers observed that, based on the photos, the proposed ATM
appears to be located where there is currently a storefront.

Mr. Knapp explained that the existing door moves toward the post office, and a
new wall will be constructed for the ATM installation.
Vice Chair Summers clarified that a new infill wall will be constructed. She asked if
the proposed elevations show the existing glazed storefront window system being
replaced by the ATM and infill wall, designed to match the older wall material.
Mr. Knapp confirmed that the ATM and in-fill wall will replace the existing glass
window. Vice Chair Summers noted that this change will make the front appear
more like the original 1912 design, with a more solid wall, and Mr. Knapp agreed,
Chair Larson acknowledged that this is a unique case, given the building’s original
1912 construction and numerous subsequent changes. While national guidelines do
not fully address such complex situations, she emphasized that the building remains
historically important. She noted that the building reflects its ongoing use as a bank
and demonstrates how banking and the building have evolved over time. Chair
Larson suggested that, rather than preserving a single historic moment, the
building’s story could be interpreted through its successive changes. She
recommended that the applicant consider incorporating interpretive elements to
highlight the building’s history and evolution, framing the historic character as
dynamic rather than static. This approach recognizes the building as historic, even if
its integrity has been altered.
Commissioner Souza remarked that the bank has been a long-standing presence
and cares for its customers. She noted that placing the ATM outside enhances
safety by making it more visible, reflecting the bank’s ongoing commitment to its
patrons.

Vice Chair Summers asked if very little would change in the corner area. Mr. Knapp
responded that visually there will be minimal change, though the interior function
will change. Vice Chair Summers agreed that from the exterior viewpoint, the
corner will change very little visually.
Chair Larson asked which option would be better for the building: installing a new
ATM facing the road under the lanai against the first wall or placing the ATM on the
side of the building with a temporary weather-protection structure for users. She
asked which option would be more intrusive to the historic structure and which
would be more difficult or impossible to undo, noting concerns about installing an
ATM into an original 1912 wall.
Mr. Knapp stated that the project involves remodeling a 1963 building that was
previously modified in 2003.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa said Ms. Valenciano did a strong job presenting the building’s
history and overall integrity. She suggested viewing the proposal in a broader
context, considering the integrity of the entire building, its location, and customer
flow, rather than focusing too narrowly on the age or integrity of a single wall.
Vice Chair Summers said the colonnade and the experience of passing through it are
the building’s defining features. She felt the large overhang would minimize the
visibility of the ATM and that preserving this aspect of the building’s integrity was
more important, noting the proposal seemed focused on customer use rather than
altering key architectural elements.
Commissioner Kikuchi-Samonte said placing the ATM on the front of the building
would feel safer than on the side street. She supported the plan as long as it does

not impact the colonnade or roof.
Chair Larson suggested incorporating historical interpretation into the project by
displaying artifacts from the bank’s past, such as old post office boxes or early
banking elements. She noted general support from the group for including historical
interpretation and that no other major concerns were raised.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa said the Commission may recommend interpretive signage,
which staff would then discuss and negotiate with the applicant. She noted that an
analysis may be required and that interpretive signage could be included as a
condition of zoning permit approval, depending on the outcome.
With no further discussion, Chair Larson called for a motion to recommend a
mandatory historical interpretation as part of the project and to approve the plans
as amended.
Chair Larson called for a 10-minute recess at 10:18 a.m., and called the meeting
back to order at 10:28 a.m.

Vice Chair Summers moved to
recommend a mandatory historical

as amended. Commissioner Souza

1. Hawai`i Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration NHPA
Section 106 Programmatic Agreement for Minor Highway Projects Statewide
Ms. Valenciano clarified that no applicant or agency was present due to budget
constraints. She explained that this item is informational only, regarding the final
draft of a programmatic agreement among HDOT, Federal Highways, and other
parties. The agreement would allow in-house Section 106 reviews for minor routine
highway projects that do not affect historic properties, streamlining the review
process. Projects are categorized into tiers one through three, with varying levels of
review required. The programmatic agreement, initiated in May 2019, is expected
to be completed in 2026. Ms. Valenciano noted the County brough this to the
Commission for awareness and that comments from the Commission can still be
submitted.
Chair Larson asked how the programmatic agreement would address or affect the
County’s historic byways.
Ms. Valenciano said she hasn’t specifically looked into the impact on historic

byways, such as the Hanalei Belt Road, but acknowledged their existence. She
noted that the project manager, Pua Aiu, may have answers and offered to follow
up and pass along any information.
Chair Larson noted that projects affecting historic properties would still undergo the
standard Section 106 process. Ms. Valenciano confirmed that this is her
understanding as well.
Chair Larson asked whether signage is included in the programmatic agreement,
noting concerns about excessive signage.
Ms. Valenciano said she did not see anything specific about signage in the summary
provided but noted it could be included in the programmatic agreement and
offered to follow up.
Chair Larson noted that DOT has its own regulations regarding signage placement
and design, which can conflict with community aesthetics and safety concerns,
particularly when there are too many signs or they are difficult to read.
Ms. Valenciano said she can pass along the concerns about signage and noted there
is a question regarding interpretive signs.
Chair Larson asked whether there is interpretive signage for the Hanalei Historic
Byway. Ms. Valenciano said she does not know.

Commissioner Souza highlighted past failures in following tree preservation
guidance, citing Po`ipū and another in Kōloa. She emphasized that education alone
is insufficient and stressed the need to review past notifications and records to
ensure County staff adhere to preservation requirements.
Chair Larson asked whether any trees are currently listed on the County’s historic
register.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa explained that the County has an ordinance allowing trees to
be designated as “exceptional trees”.
Chair Larson asked whether the historic tree designation is incorporated into the
County’s historic register, noting that historic considerations include not just
buildings but also byways, structures, and potentially trees.
Ms. Valenciano said he has not seen any specific trees listed individually on the
historic register. She noted that trees could be considered contributing elements
within a broader historic property, such as a cultural site, building, or district, but
individual groves or trees are generally not listed.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa added that historic landscapes or scenic designations could
encompass trees, so in the context of historic preservation, individual trees are
generally included within broader designations rather than listed specifically.
Chair Larson noted that when describing a historic building, the site should also be
considered. Trees, including groves, could be contributing elements to the site,
adding layers of historic significance beyond the building itself.

Ms. Valenciano explained that the nomination form for a historic property would
specify if a tree were part of the designation, providing additional protection
beyond the exceptional tree ordinance.
Commissioner Souza asked whether a list of trees designated as exceptional trees is
available.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa responded that trees listed are included in the County
ordinance itself.
Chair Larson noted that the Kaua`i Outdoor Circle website provides a link to the list
of exceptional trees on Kaua`i.
Ms. Valenciano said a copy of the list can be sent to the Commission. The list is
maintained under the Arborist Commission, included within the ordinance, and
contains several trees from Kōloa.
Ms. Higuchi Sayegusa explained that like the KHPRC, the Arborist Committee
advises the Planning Department and Public Works on exceptional trees and
relation actions. While other interests may also be involved, this committee
specifically reviews proposals affecting trees on the exceptional tree list.
Chair Larson emphasized that being on the exceptional tree list is not the only
measure of significance. Other trees or landmarks may also have historic or visual
importance and could be considered eligible for recognition even if not formally
listed.
